answer: Lahore Fort is indeed a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In the Walled City of Lahore, you can also visit other notable sites such as the Badshahi Mosque, the Shalimar Gardens, and the Wazir Khan Mosque. The Shalimar Gardens are another UNESCO World Heritage Site, known for its formal gardens, fountains, and landscaped terraces. Other significant historical sites include the Minar-e-Pakistan, the Gurdwara Dera Sahib, and the Samadhi of Ranjit Singh. There are also other sites like the Tomb of Jahangir and the Tomb of Nur Jahan. For a more modern experience, you can visit Trafalgar Square in Bahria Town, which is a replica of the famous Trafalgar Square in London.

Lahore (Punjabi: لہور; Urdu: لاہور) is Pakistan's second-largest city after Karachi and the capital of Punjab province. Located in northeastern Pakistan, Lahore is known for its historic architecture, traditional food, gardens, markets, and cultural heritage. The historic Walled City is one of its most distinctive areas, containing narrow streets, traditional neighbourhoods, historic gates, mosques, and bazaars.

Lahore has a history spanning many centuries and was an important centre under the Mughal Empire, the Sikh Empire, and British colonial rule. Visitors can explore this history at Lahore Fort, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Badshahi Mosque, one of the city's best-known Mughal-era landmarks. Nearby, the Walled City of Lahore includes the historic streets around Delhi Gate, the restored Shahi Hammam, and the colourful Wazir Khan Mosque, noted for its detailed tilework and frescoes.

Other significant historical sites include Minar-e-Pakistan, associated with the Lahore Resolution of 1940; Gurdwara Dera Sahib, an important Sikh religious site; and Samadhi of Ranjit Singh, located near Lahore Fort. The Walled City of Lahore is one of the oldest cities in the world and comprises the following places for sightseeing.

1 Lahore Fort (شاہی قلعہ, Shahi Qila). A huge structure where the Mughal and Sikh rulers built their imperial quarters. It is on the UNESCO World Heritage List. There is a small museum dedicated to the Sikh period of the 18th century. A friendly museum caretaker might agree to take you into the summer rooms underground. For non-Pakistanis is Rs 500.

2 Alamgiri Gate. The iconic entrance to the fort. Located opposite the Badshahi Mosque. (updated Feb 2017)

3 Shah Burj gate. Decorated with colored tiles. Known as the "Elephant Gate" because royal elephants would enter here. Just inside the gate is the Hathi Paer (Elephant Path) - a staircase with very wide steps so that an elephant's feet could fit on them while climbing to the upper level of the fort. The fort's wall outside this staircase is decorated with tiles including pictures of elephants. (You will also find the Alamgiri Gate occasionally called the Elephant Gate, because its two columns vaguely resemble elephant feet.) (updated Feb 2017)"},{"source_id":"Lahore","title":"Lahore","text":"Lahore

The Shalimar Gardens, another UNESCO World Heritage Site, reflect the Mughal tradition of formal gardens, fountains, and landscaped terraces.

Lahore also preserves buildings from the British colonial period, particularly along The Mall, where visitors can see historic institutions and architectural landmarks such as Lahore Museum and the General Post Office. The city offers a contrast between its older quarters and newer commercial districts, including Gulberg and Defence, which have modern shopping centres, restaurants, cafés, and hotels. Traditional bazaars, local cuisine, and cultural attractions make Lahore a destination for travellers interested in the history and everyday life of Pakistan.

Lahore (Punjabi: لہور; Urdu: لاہور‎) is Pakistan's second largest city after Karachi, and the capital of the north-eastern Punjab province. It is widely considered the country's cultural capital. The heart of Lahore is the Walled or Inner City, a very densely populated area of about one square kilometre.

Founded in legendary times, and a cultural centre for over a thousand years, Lahore has many attractions for the tourist. The Mughal and Sikh legacy survives in the Lahore Fort, Badshahi Mosque and Gurdwara, the Mall is lined with colonial-gothic buildings from the British Raj, and the suburbs of Gulberg and Defence feature palatial mansions and trendy shopping districts."},{"source_id":"Lahore > See > Walled City","title":"Walled City","text":"Lahore > See > Walled City

(You will also find the Alamgiri Gate occasionally called the Elephant Gate, because its two columns vaguely resemble elephant feet.) (updated Feb 2017)

4 Badshahi Mosque. 8:00am-8:00pm. Built by the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb, this was long the largest mosque in the world. Entrance is free, but you will be asked to pay about Rs 20 (Nov 2024) to the shoekeeper upon exit. However, it is not compulsory to pay fee for shoe storage. You can instead bring a bag to carry your shoes in after removing them at the entrance. Try going late at night, when there are few people there. Since mosques are holy places, do not wear shorts to this or any mosque; women are advised to wear long or half-sleeved clothing, and to carry a shawl so they can cover their head. Remove shoes before entering.

5 Tomb of Ranjit Singh. Tomb of this Sikh ruler of Lahore. Located next to the square between Lahore Fort and the Badshahi Mosque. (updated Feb 2017)

6 Minar-e-Pakistan. This tower, sometimes called the "Eiffel Tower of Pakistan", was built on the site where in 1940 the creation of a separate state for Muslims was recognized. Located in a park in front of the Fort and Badshahi Mosque. (updated Feb 2017)

7 Wazir Khan Mosque. An exquisite tiled mosque located near Delhi Gate."}]

Masterpieces of Mughal architecture are scattered throughout the city, even in neighborhoods that today seem a little dilapidated. Buildings and sites include:

35 Shalimar Gardens (located along the GT Road towards Wagah). A three-tiered formal garden built in the 1600s, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Rs 200 for foreigners. (updated Feb 2017)

36 Chauburji Gate (at Chauburji Chowk). An impressive, ornate 4-towered gate dating to 1646. (updated Feb 2017)

37 Tomb of Jahangir (Shahdara suburb). Built in 1637 for the Mughal emperor Jahangir. (updated Feb 2017)

38 Tomb of Nur Jahan (Shahdara suburb).  (updated Feb 2017)

There are also other sites, including tombs and mausoleums. Check this website Lahore, Pakistan: Traditional and Historical Architecture for information, plans, and photo galleries of many monuments.

39 Data Durbar (Data Darbar). A Sufi Muslim shrine to Lahore's patron saint, Hazrat Daata Ganj Bakhsh. This vast modern structure is always filled with people praying, collecting or bestowing alms, or eating at the huge charity 'langar' or soup kitchen. (updated Feb 2017)

40 Trafalgar Square (Bahria Town). A replica of the famous Trafalgar Square in London is located in the Bahria Town suburb. A Mini Egypt and a Zoo are located nearby and also worth a visit. An exquisite tiled mosque located near Delhi Gate.

8 Shahi Hammam (Imperial Baths). A Persian-style bathhouse built in 1635, restored in 2015, and covered with beautiful frescos. (updated Feb 2017)

Haveli Asif Jah.  (updated Feb 2017)

In the Mughal days, the Old City was surrounded by a 9-metre-high brick wall and had a rampart running around it which served as a protection for the city. A circular road around the rampart gave access to the city through thirteen gates. The walls were mostly destroyed by the British after the 1857 rebellion, but some of the imposing structures of the gates are still preserved. Listed clockwise, starting from Lahore Fort in the north:

9 Raushnai Gate, or the "Gate of Light" is between the royal mosque and the citadels. There is a very famous gali (row or narrow street) commonly known as the Shahi Mahala. The name Shahi has been given after the Shahi Qila. People living here are simple. There are various food shops located around the gate.

10 Masti Gate.

11 Kashmiri Gate, so called because it faces the direction of Kashmir.
